Thank you for sending your work entitled “A neural circuit mechanism for regulating motor variability during skill learning” for consideration at eLife. Your article has been favorably evaluated by Eve Marder (Senior editor) and 3 reviewers, one of whom is a member of our Board of Reviewing Editors.

The following individuals responsible for the peer review of your submission have agreed to reveal their identity: Ronald L Calabrese (BRE), Richard Mooney, (reviewer), and Samuel Sober (reviewer).

The Reviewing editor and the other reviewers discussed their comments before we reached this decision, and the Reviewing editor has assembled the following comments to help you prepare a revised submission.

The authors present a thorough electrophysiological analysis of how connectivity between HVC and RA and LMAN and RA change during the period of song acquisition and consolidation in zebra finch. They use this model to address the general issue of how motor performance and variability interact so that during acquisition variability, which is essential for learning a new skill, is reduced as performance is enhanced. The system is particularly suitable for such analyses because variability generating (LMAN) inputs and the inputs that drive learned song (HVC) separately project to the premotor area (RA). They conclude that there is no change in the variability generating inputs (LMAN) but that the song generating inputs are pruned and strengthened during song acquisition and consolidation. They then present a simple model of the system that reflects the changes in HVC and LMAN inputs to RA projection neurons observed during song maturation (learning). This model is carefully described and appropriate to the question at hand. The model is systematically explored and the modeling data supports their major conclusion that strengthening and pruning of HVC RA connections is the dominant mechanism that leads to decreased variability in performance and suggests how NMDA inputs from the viability system may enhance this process.

The paper is in general well written and clear, and the Methods are sufficiently detailed. The illustrations are clear and show all relevant data. The experiments are careful and the data convincing. The Discussion is illuminating and sets the work in a general context of motor learning that should be broadly interesting to the readers of eLife.

Detailed critiques by the expert reviewers include several points, which should be addressed by the authors in revision, but which do not require further experiments.

Reviewer #2:

In their revised submission the authors have significantly improved their manuscript by addressing some technical concerns regarding the analysis of their physiological data and by greatly expanding the scope and impact of their modeling work. In making these improvements (primarily the latter), the authors have convinced me. Although prior studies have investigated the issues they take on, the present manuscript represents a significant advance. Therefore, although it was not clear whether the original submission had sufficient impact for publication in eLife, I think that the revised manuscript represents a major contribution to the field and I think that it should be published. However there are a few things I would like to see addressed first:

1) The expanded modeling results greatly strengthen the authors' argument, however I think the presentation could be made a bit more clear. First, in Figure 6C–E, the accompanying legend, and the text in Results, I suggest that the authors more explicitly specify the baseline value relative to which the changes in LMAN input, FI gain, etc. are performed. For example, the legend to Figure 4D reads: “…(c) strengthening/weakening LMAN inputs by up to 50%”. This should specify: “… up to 50% relative to the default value of W_LMAN, which was based on our empirical measurements of single-fiber currents (see Results; Figure 4E)”. Doesn't need to be this exact text of course, but for all parameters varied in Figure 6 this type of information should be made more explicit. Also, if I'm reading Figure 6 correctly, the black lines in 6C–E, G and H all represent the “default” model, this should also perhaps be made explicit in the legend. Finally, the lightest red dashed lines are nearly invisible in 6G and H. Perhaps these could be darkened to enhance readability.

2) In the Discussion section the authors consider how elimination and strengthening of HVC inputs to RA could separately contribute to a reduction of sensitivity to LMAN drive. However, the modeling studies never dissociate these two variables (number vs strength of HVC inputs), although it seems that the authors are in a good position to do so. This section of the Discussion is therefore somewhat unsatisfying and highlights that the authors have not performed an important variation on their analysis that could yield additional insight. I think that the authors should either explore this directly using the model (by dissociating input sparsity from input strength to back up their qualitative assertions) or remove this consideration from the Discussion.

Reviewer #3:

I thoroughly enjoyed reading the greatly improved manuscript and the authors' response to the reviewers' comments, which largely addressed my concerns. This is an important study that goes to significant lengths to describe a developmental change in functional connectivity that could account for how motor variability decreases with skill learning. Overall, I believe that the study will appeal to a wide audience and serve as an extremely useful resource for those interested in neural mechanisms of motor variability and learning.

1) I was left to wonder whether the NMDA EPSC time course (i.e., decay kinetics) measured for LMAN inputs onto RA neurons are able to contribute to variability in RA neuronal firing in response to drive from HVC? The decay kinetics of NMDA-mediated currents at the LMAN to RA synapse are known to become faster with age, similar to developmental changes described at other vertebrate central synapses, especially in the mammalian neocortex. Although these changes are most often associated with sensory learning of various kinds, it would be useful to know whether a slower time course in the LMAN to RA synaptic current has an effect on RA spike variability.

2) I appreciate the authors' clarification of the novelty of their findings. I certainly agree that theirs “… is the first study to describe the functional changes in the inputs to RA from both HVC and LMAN during song development…”, and for that scope I believe the study is important and not merely incremental. And the detailed explanation they provided for why they view their characterization of the developmental changes at the HVC to RA synapse was also helpful, although I still maintain that those changes could be at least partly inferred from earlier structural and functional studies by Hermann, Kittelberger and Canady. This is not to minimize the current study's importance, but I do believe the authors could go further in integrating the earlier work into their present writing to better highlight exactly what is new here and also to more accurately place their study in the published literature.

With due respect to the authors' different perspective, I see pretty clear evidence of functional strengthening and consolidation at the HVC to RA synapse from those earlier studies when they are viewed collectively: over development, HVC bouton number in RA declines, spine density of RA projection neurons describes an inverted “U,” and the functional efficacy of the HVC to RA synapse increases. Further, Canady's serial EM reconstruction work (albeit in canary) revealed that HVC synapses are mostly (>90%) onto spines, whereas LMAN synapses are split between spines and shafts; because HVC synapses far outnumber LMAN synapses on single RA neurons (I believe the ratio was greater than 20:1, but it's been awhile since I have read it thoroughly), Canady concluded that the vast majority of inputs onto spines of RA dendrites reflected input from HVC and from other RA neurons and not from LMAN. I think it is reasonable to assume from this that the developmental changes in RA spine density reported by Kittelberger mostly reflect reorganization from those two sources and not from LMAN. This postsynaptic change is paralleled by a reduction in the frequency of putative HVC axonal boutons in RA; taken together, this seems to provide pretty clear structural evidence of a reduction in the number of HVC to RA synaptic connections with development. Lastly, those structural changes are accompanied by increased efficacy in the HVC to RA synapse, as measured by the stimulus current, EPSP onset slope relationship, which steepens significantly between 45 d juveniles and adults. At face value, this suggests to me that the HVC to RA synapse undergoes developmental consolidation in a process that involves synaptic pruning and strengthening.

Regarding determination of locus: Kittelberger's measurements of onset slope largely avoided the potential confound of polysynaptic components. He also found that spontaneous EPSC amplitudes increased (with LMAN lesions, which mimicked the developmental effects), making it less likely that the change in the stimulus-response relationship simply reflected changes in HVC fiber excitability. He noted a reduction in HVC bouton frequency along with decreased spine density and increased stimulus-response relationship. In aggregate, these findings strongly suggest to me a developmental process in which HVC synapses are pruned and strengthened, thus partially anticipating one aspect of the current study. Nonetheless, the current study goes well beyond this by providing more direct evidence of such consolidation while also providing an exact estimate of the numbers of inputs at a greater range of developmental points.

I leave it up to the authors to decide whether they see room for improvement in their discussion on these points. In my view, it takes nothing away from the current study to do so, and I do believe that a more balanced discussion of the relationship of the current study to this earlier work would be an improvement.

results.result: Motor skill learning is characterized by improved performance and reduced motor variability, with variability being beneficial early in learning for exploration but detrimental for expert performance.
results.evaluation: Claims C1, C7, C8, and C9 establish the general framework of motor skill learning based on well-established knowledge in the field, supported by appropriate citations (Lee et al., 1999; Park et al., 2013; Sutton and Barto, 1998; Tumer and Brainard, 2007; Wu et al., 2014). These claims provide the conceptual foundation for the study.

results.result: The neural circuit mechanisms that regulate motor variability as a function of learning have not been identified, representing a gap in knowledge that this study aims to address.
results.evaluation: Claims C2, C10, C22, C24, and C25 collectively establish the knowledge gap motivating the study. These are statements about the state of the field at the time of the study and are appropriately supported by the literature review.

results.result: The zebra finch song system provides a unique model for studying motor learning, with distinct circuits for learned song production (VMP: HVC-RA) and variability induction (AFP: LMAN), which converge on RA and show developmental changes during song learning.
results.evaluation: Claims C3-C20 and C29-C37 establish the zebra finch song system as a model for motor learning, describing the functional organization of the VMP and AFP pathways. These claims are well-supported by extensive citations to prior work and represent established knowledge about the songbird system. The characterization of developmental stages (C29-C31) is also well-documented.

results.result: HVC-RA connections undergo significant strengthening and pruning during song development, with single fiber currents increasing with age, MAX currents showing a non-monotonic pattern (increasing then decreasing), and the number of HVC inputs first increasing then decreasing substantially.
results.evaluation: Claims C4, C26, and C40-C52 describe the main experimental findings regarding HVC-RA connectivity changes. The data are well-documented in Figure 3 and Tables, with appropriate statistical tests (Mann-Whitney-Wilcoxon tests, Student's t-tests) showing significant differences across age groups. The log-normal distribution fits (C40) are appropriate for synaptic weight distributions. Sample sizes are adequate (72-120 single fibers across 24-39 birds per age group). The non-monotonic pattern of MAX currents (C49-C50) is particularly interesting and well-supported statistically.

results.result: Inputs from LMAN to RA remain largely unchanged throughout song development, with no significant changes in single fiber strength, MAX currents, or number of inputs, though there is a small decrease in the AMPA:NMDA ratio.
results.evaluation: Claims C5, C27, and C53-C64 describe the stability of LMAN-RA connections across development. The data are presented in Figure 4 and Table 2 with appropriate statistical tests showing no significant differences in most measures (p > 0.1 for SF distributions, p > 0.25 for MAX currents). The small change in AMPA:NMDA ratio (C59-C61) is statistically significant (p < 0.001) but modest in magnitude. Sample sizes are adequate (38-45 single fibers across 7-13 birds per age group). The consistency with prior work (C61) strengthens the findings.

results.result: The intrinsic excitability of RA projection neurons, including spike-frequency adaptation and input/output gain, remains largely unchanged across song development.
results.evaluation: Claims C65-C69 describe the intrinsic properties of RA neurons across development. The data in Figure 5 show no significant differences in adaptation magnitude or F-I curve slopes across age groups (p > 0.05), consistent with prior studies (Kittelberger and Mooney, 1999). The recordings at 35°C provide more physiological conditions than prior studies. Sample sizes are modest (9-10 cells per age group) but adequate for these measurements.

results.result: Strengthening and pruning of HVC-RA connections reduces the sensitivity of motor control circuits to variable input and neural noise, and is the dominant mechanism underlying learning-related reduction in vocal variability.
results.evaluation: Claims C6, C28, and C72-C87 describe the main conclusions from the computational modeling. The model (Figure 6) shows that strengthening and pruning of HVC-RA connections can account for the observed reduction in variability, with the two processes acting synergistically (C74-C75). The model parameters are derived from experimental data (Figures 3-5), and the results closely match in vivo observations (Ölveczky et al., 2011). The model is appropriately simple and focused on testing specific hypotheses about circuit mechanisms.

results.result: Alternative mechanisms for reducing variability, including weakening LMAN input, changing NMDA:AMPA ratios, or altering RA neuron gain, have minimal effects compared to HVC-RA strengthening and pruning.
results.evaluation: Claims C76-C79 describe modeling results testing alternative mechanisms. The simulations (Figure 6C-E) show that these mechanisms explain less than 20% of the variability reduction (C76) or have minimal effects (C78-C79). These results are important for ruling out alternative explanations and supporting the main conclusion that HVC-RA reorganization is dominant.

results.result: Changes in LMAN firing patterns, including increased burstiness or song-locking, can affect RA variability, with burstier firing increasing variability and more song-locked firing decreasing variability.
results.evaluation: Claims C80-C84 describe modeling results on LMAN firing patterns. The simulations (Figure 6F-H) are based on prior observations (Kao et al., 2008; Ölveczky et al., 2005) and show expected effects. However, whether RA-projecting LMAN neurons actually show increased song-locking in adults remains to be experimentally tested (C83), making this a prediction rather than a confirmed mechanism.

results.result: The mechanism for coupling motor variability and skill learning through strengthening and pruning of action-specific connections may apply broadly to mammalian motor learning, offering a general circuit-level explanation for learning-related reduction in motor variability.
results.evaluation: Claims C91-C92 and C94-C96 propose that the mechanism may generalize to mammalian systems, supported by citations showing similar synaptic changes in mammalian cortex. However, this remains speculative (C92 is explicitly labeled as speculation) as direct experimental evidence in mammalian motor learning is not provided. The proposal is reasonable and testable but requires future work for validation.

results.result: The proposed mechanism predicts that syllables farther from their target should be more variable, which is consistent with prior observations showing a correlation between syllable distance from target and variability.
results.evaluation: Claims C97-C100 connect the proposed mechanism to prior observations (Ravbar et al., 2012). The prediction (C98) follows logically from the model, and the consistency with prior data (C99) provides supporting evidence. This represents a successful post-hoc explanation of existing observations.

results.result: The abundance of HVC-RA connections during sensorimotor learning provides a large substrate for exploration and modification, which then decreases as learning proceeds, making acquired behavior more robust to change.
results.evaluation: Claims C101-C103 provide a functional interpretation of the observed changes in HVC-RA connectivity. This interpretation is logical and consistent with the data (Figure 3G) showing the non-monotonic pattern of input numbers. The reasoning connects circuit structure to function in a plausible way.

results.result: Each RA neuron receives approximately 11-26 inputs from HVC (age-dependent) and 2-3 inputs from LMAN (age-independent) in the slice preparation, consistent with structural studies and functional requirements.
results.evaluation: Claims C119-C123 provide estimates of connectivity that are derived from the experimental data (MAX/SF ratios) and consistent with prior structural studies (Canady et al., 1988; Herrmann and Arnold, 1991). The authors appropriately note these are lower bounds due to potential loss of inputs in slices. The functional interpretation (C122-C123) is reasonable.

results.result: Pruning of HVC-RA connections reduces depolarizing events in RA neurons, limiting LMAN's effectiveness through NMDAR voltage-dependence, while strengthening of HVC inputs saturates RA neurons, further reducing LMAN's capacity to modulate firing.
results.evaluation: Claims C124-C130 provide mechanistic explanations for how HVC-RA reorganization reduces LMAN's effectiveness. The reasoning is based on well-established NMDAR properties (C125, supported by citations) and prior observations of RA neuron hyperpolarization and firing patterns (C127-C128, supported by citations). The logic is sound and consistent with the experimental findings.

results.result: Modulating the burstiness of LMAN neurons could be an effective mechanism for fast and context-dependent regulation of vocal variability, as suggested by differences between female-directed and undirected song.
results.evaluation: Claims C131-C132 connect the modeling results to behavioral observations. The observation that female-directed song is more stereotyped and associated with less bursty LMAN firing (C131, supported by citations) is consistent with the modeling prediction that burstier firing increases variability. This provides indirect support for the mechanism.

results.result: The experimental approach used whole-cell patch-clamp recordings in acute brain slices from 124 male zebra finches across three developmental stages, with separate slice preparations optimized for HVC and LMAN inputs.
results.evaluation: Claims C107-C118 describe the methodological approach. The methods are well-established and appropriate for the questions being asked. The use of different slice orientations for HVC vs LMAN inputs (C110) is justified by the different entry planes of these fibers (C38). The sample sizes are adequate. The methodological details are clearly described in the Materials and Methods section.
